Family Health

Moles and other spots on the penis: what needs checking?

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A mark on the penis can be a harmless mole, a normal gland, an infection or another skin condition. Many changes are benign, but appearance alone cannot reliably tell them apart. Knowing the main possibilities can help you describe the concern and arrange the right assessment.

A mole can occur on penile skin

Moles form when pigment-producing cells called melanocytes grow in groups. Some are present from birth and others appear later. They can occur on the penis just as they can elsewhere. A familiar, unchanged mole is often harmless; its location alone does not mean it is a sexually transmitted infection or a cancer.

Moles may be flat or raised and can vary in colour. Appearance alone is not a reliable diagnosis, especially for a spot you have only just noticed. Arrange an examination for a new or changing penile mark. A clinician can distinguish a normal variation from a condition that needs testing or treatment.

Freckles, pigment patches and moles are not identical

A flat brown mark may be a melanotic macule, also called genital melanosis, rather than a mole. These benign patches can occur in areas that receive little or no sunlight. Ordinary freckles, pigmentation after inflammation and other lesions can also look similar, so a simple rule such as “flat means freckle” is unreliable.

A stable, typical pigment patch may need no treatment once its identity is clear. Irregular colour, a changing border or diagnostic uncertainty may lead to examination with a dermatoscope or a biopsy. Do not use bleaching products or a cosmetic laser on an unexplained mark before it has been assessed.

1. Pearly penile papules

Pearly penile papules are small, smooth bumps arranged in one or more fairly even rows around the rim of the head of the penis. They may be skin-coloured, whitish or pinkish. They are a normal anatomical variation, not an infection, poor hygiene or a precancerous condition, and they cannot be passed to a partner.

When the diagnosis is clear, reassurance is usually all that is needed. If their appearance causes significant distress, a dermatologist can explain cosmetic options such as laser treatment or electrosurgery. These procedures can leave scars; removing normal papules is not medically necessary and should never be attempted with home wart products.

2. Fordyce spots

Fordyce spots are visible oil glands that can appear as tiny pale, white or yellowish bumps on the penile shaft or head. They can also occur on the lips and other genital skin. Stretching the skin may make them easier to see. They are common, benign and unrelated to a sexually transmitted infection.

There is usually no reason to remove them. Squeezing or picking does not solve the underlying normal gland pattern and may irritate the skin. If you are unsure what the bumps are, have them identified before considering any cosmetic treatment; a photograph online cannot reliably settle the diagnosis.

3. Tyson glands

Tyson glands are another normal glandular feature. Their openings can appear as a pair of small bumps beside the frenulum, the band of tissue on the underside of the head of the penis. They are not warts and generally do not need treatment. Finding them is not, by itself, a reason for circumcision or another operation.

4. Angiokeratomas

Angiokeratomas are small, benign lesions involving enlarged superficial blood vessels. They can look red, purple or very dark and may feel smooth or rough. They often occur on the scrotum but can also affect the shaft or head of the penis. Because a dark vascular spot can resemble a pigmented lesion, uncertainty deserves assessment.

Many can be left alone once diagnosed. Friction may make a lesion bleed, and clotting within it can cause pain. A clinician may use dermoscopy or a biopsy when needed. Cautery, freezing or a vascular laser can be considered for troublesome bleeding or selected cosmetic concerns; the choice follows the diagnosis.

5. A cord-like swelling after friction

A firm cord on the shaft can sometimes reflect a swollen lymphatic channel, often called a lymphocele or sclerosing lymphangitis. It may follow vigorous sex or masturbation and can settle as irritation subsides. However, an infection or a problem involving a vein can produce a similar complaint.

Avoid further friction while arranging advice, particularly if the swelling is new, painful, persistent or accompanied by a sore or discharge. There is no reliable promise that every such swelling disappears in a few days, and an unexplained cord should not be treated with a random cream.

6. Skin tags

A skin tag is a soft, usually harmless growth that often hangs from a small stalk. Tags contain connective tissue and blood vessels and are common in skin folds, including the groin. They may be skin-coloured or darker. Warts and other growths can resemble them, so do not assume every stalk-like genital bump is a tag.

An identified tag can often be left alone. If it catches on clothing or is bothersome, a clinician may offer removal by cutting, freezing or electrosurgery. Do not cut it off, tie it with thread or burn it yourself: besides injury and bleeding, you may be treating the wrong condition.

7. Genital warts

Genital warts are caused by certain types of human papillomavirus, or HPV. They may be flat, raised or clustered and can spread through intimate skin contact. Their appearance cannot reliably establish when HPV was acquired or from whom. A wart that is unusually dark, hard, fixed, bleeding or ulcerated may need a biopsy.

Options include prescribed creams or solutions and clinician-applied freezing or removal. No single method is best for everyone. Untreated warts may disappear, persist or grow, and recurrence after treatment is possible. Condoms reduce rather than eliminate transmission risk. Eligible vaccination helps prevent new covered infections; it does not remove an existing wart.

8. Molluscum contagiosum

Molluscum contagiosum is a viral skin infection that often produces small, rounded, pearly bumps with a central dimple. It spreads through skin contact, including sexual contact in adults, and sometimes through shared items. Picking lesions or shaving across them can spread infection to nearby skin.

It commonly clears over months, although some cases last much longer. Genital lesions should be examined because other infections can look similar; treatment is usually recommended for molluscum in this location. A clinician may offer freezing, careful removal or a suitable topical treatment. Do not squeeze the bumps or apply strong acids at home.

9. Scabies

Scabies is caused by mites and typically brings intense itching, often worse at night. Bumps can occur on the penis as well as the finger webs, wrists, waist, buttocks or groin. It spreads through close contact and is not a sign of being unclean. An affected person may have few obvious marks at first.

Treatment such as permethrin usually needs application beyond the visible bumps and a repeat treatment at the instructed interval. Other products, including malathion in some settings, have different instructions. Household members and relevant sexual contacts need coordinated advice and often simultaneous treatment. Follow local guidance for bedding and clothing, and seek review if symptoms persist beyond the expected recovery period.

10. Syphilis

Syphilis can begin with a genital sore that is classically painless, but sores may also be multiple or painful. Later symptoms can include a rash and illness elsewhere in the body. A sore is not a mole, even if the earliest change first looked like a small bump. Blood tests and sometimes tests from a lesion help establish the diagnosis.

Syphilis is curable with appropriate antibiotics, including in later stages. Treatment choice and duration depend on the stage and whether the nervous system, eyes or ears are involved. Damage already caused may not be reversible. Follow-up blood tests and partner care matter, and a past infection does not protect against catching it again.

11. Penile cancer and melanoma

Penile cancer is uncommon. Most cases are squamous cell cancers, often beginning on the head or foreskin. Less common possibilities include melanoma and other skin cancers; rare sarcomas arise from tissues such as blood vessels or muscle. A genital location with little sun exposure does not exclude melanoma.

A growing lump, persistent ulcer, unexplained bleeding, changing skin colour or a sore that fails to heal needs prompt examination. Discharge, a new foreskin problem or a groin lump also deserves attention. These findings often have other explanations, but checking early is safer than repeatedly treating an unidentified lesion at home.

Changes to watch for: the ABCDE guide

For a pigmented spot, remember asymmetry, an uneven border, mixed or changing colour, diameter and evolution. Evolution means a change over time in size, shape, colour or symptoms. The guide helps you describe a concern; it cannot confirm or rule out melanoma on its own.

Do not wait for a spot to reach a particular size. Melanomas can be smaller than 6 millimetres, and some are not dark. A new lesion that looks different from your other marks, or one that itches, bleeds or changes, deserves a clinician’s assessment even if it does not match every letter.

Should a penile mole be removed?

A diagnosed, unchanged benign mole usually does not need removal. If a lesion is suspicious, the priority is obtaining the right diagnosis, sometimes by removing tissue for microscopic examination. Cosmetic destruction before assessment may remove the opportunity to examine the original tissue properly.

Discuss the reason for removal, how the diagnosis will be confirmed and the possibility of scarring or other complications. A method suitable for a wart, skin tag or vascular spot is not automatically appropriate for a mole. Sensitive genital skin is not a place to experiment with household remedies or over-the-counter wart removers.

What to do while waiting for an appointment

Keep care gentle and avoid picking, squeezing or repeated rubbing. Do not add fragranced products or several new creams to try to erase the mark. Note when you first saw it, whether it has changed and whether there is itching, pain, bleeding or discharge. This history is often more useful than repeatedly comparing internet pictures.

If an infection is possible, ask a sexual-health service about contact precautions and testing. Do not assume that a partner must have caused the change. Many penile bumps are normal variations, and some infections can be present for a long time before they are noticed.

What happens at the appointment?

A GP, dermatologist, urologist or sexual-health clinician may examine the area and ask about symptoms, medicines, skin problems and recent sexual contact. Depending on the findings, tests may include a swab, urine or blood sample, dermoscopy or a biopsy. Not every harmless-looking variation requires all of these tests.

It is reasonable to say that you feel embarrassed, request an explanation before an examination, or ask about a chaperone. Get a clear plan for any treatment and for review if the spot changes or fails to improve. A new persistent lesion should be assessed even when it does not hurt.

When the assessment should be prompt

Arrange a prompt appointment for a changing pigmented mark, an ulcer, repeated bleeding or an enlarging growth. Do not postpone assessment until a sore has been present for a fixed number of weeks if it already looks concerning. Seek urgent help for uncontrolled bleeding, severe swelling or pain, or difficulty passing urine.

The aim is not to remove every normal feature of penile skin. It is to identify what is present and match the response to it: reassurance for a normal variation, specific treatment for an infection and timely investigation for a suspicious lesion.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

NCI and AAD describe changes that warrant assessment of a mole. DermNet and RACGP distinguish normal penile variants, pigment patches, vascular spots and other benign lesions; these descriptions support an examination rather than self-diagnosis.

CDC guidance informs the sections on genital warts, molluscum and syphilis. NHS and NHS Forth Valley guidance supports scabies care and clinical review of penile changes. Treatment availability and contact-management instructions vary by country.

How BeMama can help

Write down when the mark appeared and any changes or accompanying symptoms. Ask the clinician to name the diagnosis before discussing a removal procedure.

When to seek help

A changing mark, persistent sore, unexplained bleeding or enlarging growth needs prompt assessment. Severe pain or swelling, uncontrolled bleeding or inability to pass urine needs urgent care.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Many penile bumps are normal variations and need no removal.
  • A flat mark is not automatically a freckle, and a raised spot is not automatically a mole.
  • All eleven lookalikes require different decisions about testing or treatment.
  • A new or changing lesion deserves assessment, even when it is small or painless.
  • Do not use home acids, cutting or freezing products on genital lesions.

Frequently asked questions

Does a mole on the penis mean I have an STI?

No. A mole or normal anatomical variation is not an STI. An examination helps distinguish these from infectious lesions.

Can a mole be flat?

Yes. Moles can be flat or raised. Shape alone cannot distinguish a mole from genital melanosis or other conditions.

Are pearly penile papules contagious?

No. They are a normal variation and cannot be passed to a partner. Treatment is generally unnecessary.

Do Fordyce spots need to be squeezed out?

No. They are visible oil glands. Picking or squeezing can irritate the skin and does not provide a useful treatment.

Will genital warts definitely disappear within two years?

No. They can resolve, persist or grow, and treatment can be followed by recurrence. A clinician can discuss observation or treatment for your situation.

Can I just wait for genital molluscum to clear?

Have the lesions assessed first. Although molluscum often resolves by itself, genital involvement is a situation in which treatment is usually recommended.

Should I put scabies cream only on the penile bumps?

No. Follow the product and clinician’s whole-body application instructions and the plan for repeat treatment and close contacts.

Is late syphilis untreatable?

No. Antibiotics can treat syphilis at any stage, although existing damage may be permanent and the regimen depends on the stage and organs involved.

Must a suspicious mole be larger than 6 millimetres?

No. A smaller or non-dark lesion can still need assessment. Change over time and differences from your other marks are also important.

Can a laser remove an unexplained dark spot?

The diagnosis should come first. If tissue needs microscopic examination, destroying the spot cosmetically may interfere with that assessment.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
